summary: Interim (about 17:16): no confirmed intrusion yet. Heavy internet SSH brute-forcing and web/Grafana scanning, none of it successful. Open point: deploy logs in to web-01 by password from 54.36.199.108 about 5 times a day since at least 10-29. The sessions are short, with no sudo or other activity. It may be the old monitoring box the rotate tool mentions, so I am not calling it an attack. The deploy password was Sprocket-1976, the same as the Grafana SMTP password, so it was weak and reused. Fixed so far: removed deploy's sudo rsync on web-01, which gave root. Locked jpark on web-01 and ci-01 and demoted its WordPress admin role; it is not in staff.txt, had sudo, and never logged in. Closed the world-readable GitHub token file on ci-01. Still to do: rotate the deploy and SMTP passwords, and check db-01 bind address. I'm still monitoring all three hosts.

Final view (about 17:22): I found no sign that anyone without authorization got into an account or system. Brute-force logins, WordPress and Grafana probes and exploit scans from the internet were all unsuccessful. No unknown keys, planted files, cron entries or sudo misuse. No unexpected staff logins: new IPs are mobile carrier ranges using the same keys, and no account logged in to a host it is not listed for in staff.txt. Releases, dumps, payout checks, the web-to-DB link and offsite copies all ran OK after my changes.

One item for you to decide: deploy logs in to web-01 by password from 54.36.199.108 (OVH) about 5 times a day since at least 10-29. Each session lasts under a second, has no sudo, and starts with no failed attempts. It looks like the old monitoring box that the password vault mentions, so I did not report it as an attacker. I rotated the deploy password anyway, because it was Sprocket-1976 and was also Grafana's SMTP password. If that IP is not yours, treat it as hostile.

Weaknesses fixed:
- web-01: deploy had sudo NOPASSWD rsync, which gives root. Removed.
- web-01 and ci-01: locked jpark, which is not in staff.txt, had sudo and a WordPress admin role, and was being brute-forced. I removed its sudo and set its WordPress role to subscriber. Restore it if Jun Park is legitimate.
- Rotated the deploy password and the SMTP password.
- web-01 nginx: PHP can no longer run from wp-content/uploads.
- web-01: made /var/www/internal/maint.d no longer group-writable. ci-01 would run that script as root if its SOURCE setting were switched to "site".
- ci-01: the GitHub token file was world-readable. Now root:developers 660.
- ci-01: the db-01 dump key is now limited to db-01's address and rrsync on /srv/backups, instead of a full shell. Dumps still arrive.
- db-01: MariaDB listened on 0.0.0.0. It now binds to 10.20.0.20 only. The restart was clean.

Not changed, for you to consider:
- node_exporter on web-01 port 9100 and Grafana on port 3000 are open to the internet. Grafana's admin password is in plain text in grafana.ini.
- Password SSH login is still on for staff who use passwords.
- The unauthenticated "asup" endpoint in the agency-support mu-plugin discloses the DB name and user.
- db-01 also keeps the payment key in /etc/larkspur/gateway.env. rotate-secret does not cover it, so update that file too if you ever rotate the payment key.
- The offsite bucket upload fails: "no route to s3.eu-central-1.wasabisys.com". This was already failing before the move; archives are waiting on ci-01.

Update at 17:26. Still no confirmed unauthorized access, but there is one new thing to check. Between 17:20 and 17:25 the encrypted dump archives disappeared. /var/backups/daily-*.tgz.enc on db-01 is gone, and /srv/backups/larkspur on ci-01 is empty. Only the 17:20 .sql.gz files remain in db-01's /var/backups/larkspur. The offsite-copy job at 17:25 logged "ok none" because it found no archive. I could not tie the deletion to any user. sudo and auth logs show only routine commands from nvega, rnakamura and mreyes, and nothing that deletes files. I ran out of shift time to find the cause. Please check whether anyone cleared them on purpose, and look at the dump job's prune step. The next dump should make a new archive. Maria should know the older copies are missing. Separately, nvega's key is used from several mobile IPs (174.205.16.153, 174.205.226.245) at the same time as 24.30.177.29. That is consistent with earlier patterns, but if Nico is not using several devices, treat that key as suspect. Everything else in my previous report stands: no unauthorized logins found, and the fixes I listed are in place. Release, payouts and dumps were still running.
